KEY MESSAGE 1... 
A weak cold front will continue to settle south 
toward the Ohio River this morning as weak surface high pressure 
builds across the southern Great Lakes. This will allow dew points 
to run about 10 degrees cooler today making for noticeably less 
humid conditions, but temperatures will remain very warm with highs 
in the mid/upper 80s again.

The well advertised very active pattern will begin tonight as the 
surface high drifts east and allows the front to lift back north as 
a warm front in response to a mid/upper shortwave dropping into the 
Upper Midwest. This shortwave will be one of many that will progress 
through a WNW mid/upper flow pattern between a broad ridge
covering the southern Plains and Mid Mississippi Valley and
broad trough over southern Canada and the Great Lakes. Each
shortwave will interact with the frontal boundary as it becomes
quasi-stationary across the southern Great Lakes and Ohio 
Valley regions, bringing multiple rounds of convection tonight 
through Wednesday. Unfortunately, the forecast has become even 
more uncertain in terms of the timing, location, and intensity 
of each round of convection since each thunderstorm complex 
(MCS) will move the location of the front and also lay down 
outflow boundaries which will affect the evolution and track of 
future complexes. Despite the high uncertainty and resulting low
confidence forecast, attempted to describe some individual 
periods below.

Tonight and Monday morning: This period is trending somewhat 
more impactful, and the Day 1 SPC Marginal Risk (1 of 5) for 
severe weather has been expanded through the entire area 
tonight, and a Slight Risk (2 of 5) has been added to NW Ohio,
along with a small expansion of the WPC Day 1 Slight Risk for 
excessive rainfall into more of NW Ohio. The initial shortwave
moving into the Upper Midwest tonight will ignite an MCS over
the western Great Lakes this evening, where a 30-40 knot low-
level jet will focus strong warm/moist/theta e advection into 
the frontal boundary. The past few runs of the HREF members and
RRFS have struggled with the evolution and track of this MCS
(and will continue to do so in this entire pattern), but
consensus is becoming more aligned with the idea that it will
move at least into NW Ohio late tonight and possibly roll
through the lakeshore counties in the pre-dawn hours Monday
morning along the retreating frontal boundary. Instability will
be weaker tonight and early Monday morning compared to the
source region for this complex to the west, so the most intense
portion of the system may dive south through Illinois and
Indiana, but slowly increasing low-level moisture and
instability through the night coupled with increasing mid-level
flow ahead of the approaching shortwave should be enough to
support some damaging wind risk, and PWATs rising back to 1.5 to
2 inches definitely support torrential rainfall with any
thunderstorms. So, potential is growing for thunderstorms late
tonight and early Monday morning to have decent organization 
and produce some scattered wind damage and heavy rainfall.

Monday afternoon and Monday night: This period is trending drier
since the greater coverage and organization of the convection
early Monday morning should push the boundary back southwest and
also lay down outflow boundaries. This will likely cause new
convection to initiate farther southwest Monday evening and
Monday night. The shortwave will continue to progress through 
the central Great Lakes Monday afternoon and evening, with a
30-40 knot low-level jet response focusing warm/moist/theta e
advection into the front and outflow boundaries. This will
ignite another MCS Monday evening or early Monday night, but 
consensus is growing that the bulk of the activity will be 
confined to areas along and south of a Findlay to Mount Vernon 
line, and some HREF members even have it entirely southwest of
our CWA. While the threat of organized convection is decreasing
for most of our area Monday evening through Monday night,
noteworthy deep layer effective shear of 35-40 knots along with
the low-level jet aligned increasingly parallel to the main
boundary supports both severe weather (mainly damaging winds but
a couple of tornadoes) and torrential rainfall/flash flooding
from backbuilding convection wherever it develops and tracks. It
will be important to continue to check the latest forecast for
Monday evening and Monday night since the convection will be
significant wherever it ends up being.

Tuesday and Tuesday night: Uncertainty becomes really high by
the time we get to this period of the forecast, but the synoptic
frontal boundary remaining quasi-stationary and wavering around

appears to be one or two additional shortwaves will ignite 
additional scattered convection during peak heating and MCS
